source: Schneider & Schramm (2025) The Wisdom of Deliberating AI Crowds
finding: Direct test of one feedback round versus independent forecasts then median. Gain only for mixed-model groups with shared information.
numbers: 202 resolved Metaculus binary questions; GPT-5, Claude Sonnet 4.5, Gemini 2.5 Pro; one deliberation round; median aggregate. Log loss independent vs deliberative: diverse/distributed 0.475 to 0.453 (p 0.18); diverse/shared 0.501 to 0.481 (p 0.017); homogeneous/distributed 0.517 to 0.525 (p 0.72); homogeneous/shared 0.525 to 0.545 (p 0.14).
limits: One round only. No token or cost matching. No multiple-comparison correction. Only one cell of four significant. Methods text has a sample-size inconsistency (606 observations).
agent_relevance: Closest answer to gap 1: a feedback round adds a small gain (about 4% relative) only across different models, and none or slightly negative for copies of one model. Not equal-token.

source: Schneider & Schramm (2025) The Wisdom of Deliberating AI Crowds (Brier and power)
finding: Brier check agrees with log loss. Study was underpowered for the distributed-information cells; extra evidence did not help the independent stage.
numbers: Brier change diverse/shared -0.009 (p 0.014), diverse/distributed -0.008 (p 0.26), homogeneous +0.001 (p 0.90) and +0.007 (p 0.12). Minimum detectable effect about 0.047 log loss vs observed 0.022. Evidence ablation: full info -0.038 (p 0.33) diverse, -0.008 (p 0.83) homogeneous. Gemini homogeneous groups worsened by +0.047 and +0.052 (not significant).
limits: Info summaries were written by Gemini 2.5 Pro, which is also a forecaster. Not powered for per-model results.
agent_relevance: Treat feedback gains as small and fragile. Any agent that adds a feedback step must be tested against the independent-then-average arm at equal calls.

source: InfoDelphi, Polymarket forecasting (arXiv 2607.01661, via AlphaXiv markdown)
finding: Round ablation for a Delphi-style multi-agent forecaster: two rounds beat one, three rounds are worse.
numbers: 375 Polymarket binary markets, fixed retrieved evidence, GPT-5.4-mini. Brier/accuracy: R=1 0.206/74.1%; R=2 0.178/77.9%; R=3 0.196/75.7%. Rationale sharing removed: 0.211/70.4%. Uniform weights 0.196; confidence-weighted 0.178.
limits: Single run for main and ablation tables; cross-model table gives GPT-5.4-mini iterative 0.189 +/- 0.009, worse than headline 0.178, so headline may be a favourable run. Read via a summary page, not the PDF. Not compute-matched: 9 calls per question vs baselines with 3 to 10.
agent_relevance: First round-count ablation found for gap 1. Rounds help once, then reverse. Gain is mostly from sharing rationales. Still not equal-token against independent samples plus averaging.

finding: Against 11 baselines on the same evidence, the Delphi arm had best Brier. Backend change moves results more than rounds do for some models. Heterogeneous panels were not tested.
numbers: Baselines Brier: zero-shot 0.201, CoT 0.216, self-consistency 0.221 (5 samples), standard debate 0.202/73.9%, crowd ensemble 0.245, MoA 0.220. DeepSeek-V3.2 independent 0.184 to iterative 0.163; Llama-4-Scout 0.209 to 0.204 (0.005 gain). Wilcoxon vs debate p 0.021. Cost per run $12.66 (GPT-5.4-mini), $3.51 (DeepSeek), $0.51 (Llama).
limits: Zero-shot (0.201) beats most elaborate baselines on Brier, so the Delphi margin over zero-shot is 0.023. Every agent used one model. Echo-chamber failure case: 0.995 to 0.998 on a question resolving NO.
agent_relevance: Small models gain little from iteration. Zero-shot is a strong baseline that our agent must beat. Gap 9 not answered here: all agents were the same model.

source: Evaluating LLMs on Real-World Forecasting Against Expert Forecasters (arXiv 2507.04562v3)
finding: A narrative prompt (model writes a scripted discussion of the outcome) usually scored worse than a direct range-first prompt.
numbers: 334 main questions and 130 hold-out; five calls per question, median ensemble Brier. Direct vs narrative: o3 0.1352 vs 0.1985; GPT-4.1 0.1542 vs 0.1842; DeepSeek-v3 0.1798 vs 0.2689; Claude 3.6 Sonnet 0.1810 vs 0.2345; GPT-4o 0.1883 vs 0.1940. Narrative better only for Qwen3-235B (0.1871 vs 0.1923). Expert forecasters mean Brier 0.1573 on 157 questions.
limits: Narrative here is a Silver and Tetlock dialogue, not Kahn style scenario branches. No token matching. The paper text calls hold-out narrative results slightly better but its own table shows o3 worse (0.1544 vs 0.1375).
agent_relevance: Gap 2 partly answered: story framing hurt probability accuracy for 11 of 12 models. A branch-then-probability scheme is still untested. Do not assume narrative helps scoring.

source: Rowe & Wright (1999) The Delphi technique as a forecasting tool: issues and analysis (abstract via search result)
finding: Review of empirical Delphi studies: Delphi groups beat statistical groups, with no consistent edge over other structured procedures.
numbers: Vote count 12 to 2 with 2 ties vs statistical groups; 5 to 1 with 2 ties vs standard interacting groups. Abstract and search snippet only.
limits: Full text blocked (sciencedirect 403). Authors warn that lab Delphi differs from original Delphi concept. Round-level accuracy not seen.
agent_relevance: Supports structure, not rounds as such. Vote counts, not effect sizes.

finding: Secondary page lists the Dalkey and Helmer 1963 citation and the Basu and Schroeder 1977 case but gives no round-by-round numbers; calls overall accuracy mixed.
numbers: Basu and Schroeder: 3 to 4% error for first two years of sales vs 10 to 15% quantitative and about 20% unstructured. Five-round eLAC Delphi had 1,454 contributions.
limits: Primary Dalkey and Helmer RM-727 and Sackman 1974 report not opened: RAND site returned 403 for every URL tried.
agent_relevance: Gap 3 stays open. Cite the 1963 paper only through secondary sources.

finding: Evidence that scenario traditions forecast well is anecdotal and mostly from Shell.
numbers: Diffenbach 1983 survey: alternate scenarios used by 68% of large organisations (adoption, not accuracy). Wack began Shell scenario work in 1971. De Geus audit early 1980s blamed decisions after the scenarios.
limits: Page reports no firm-performance study and does not say Shell predicted the 1973 shock.
agent_relevance: Gap 5 mostly open. Hit rates were not found. The claim that scenarios work rests on anecdote.

finding: Date and scope facts for Kahn. Year 2000 book is 1967 with Wiener; Table XVIII lists 100 technical innovations very likely by 2000. No accuracy audit given.
numbers: Thinking About the Unthinkable 1962 (Horizon); On Escalation 1965 (Praeger). Escalation ladder 16 steps (1962) to 44 steps (1965). On Thermonuclear War sold 14,000 in two months.
limits: This page gives 1962 for Thinking About the Unthinkable; the earlier 1965 date likely belongs to On Escalation, but that is not confirmed from a primary source. No hit-rate count found.
agent_relevance: Mostly settles correction 4 in critique (1962 per this page). Gap 5 Kahn hit rate stays open.

finding: Cross-consistency assessment removes illogical configurations from a grid; no validation evidence or AI support is described.
numbers: Bread example: six categories with four options each. 5^6 = 15,625 raw configurations; the page gives no reduced count.
limits: Ritchey 1998 and 2006 are cited but were not opened.
agent_relevance: Gap 4: no LLM-run cross-consistency evidence. Plan to measure it ourselves.

source: arXiv search and web search for LLM morphological box or cross-consistency
finding: Negative search: first 10 arXiv results for morphological analysis LLM were all about linguistic or cell morphology. One web search returned only NLP morphology papers.
limits: Not exhaustive. arXiv API returned empty bodies and other arXiv search phrasings returned zero results, so recall is low. Web search budget ran out.
agent_relevance: Treat gap 4 as open: absence of evidence only.

source: Soleimani (2025) LLM macro stress scenarios (arXiv 2512.07867), re-read for mitigations
finding: Mitigations in the paper for prompt-set severity: require both levels and changes and reconcile them against a fixed baseline. Both checks caught failures that plausibility rules missed.
numbers: GPT model: 838 of 840 scenarios accepted. Removing prompted severity bands made recession about 1.6 pp milder. Llama-3.1-8B: 744 accepted (11.4% rejected), 4 to 7 times more dispersed, contradicted its own stated changes in 90% of cases.
quote: use LLMs for narrative and sector elicitation around a prescribed severity path
limits: Eta-squared table not in the text I could read. Hard plausibility gate barely binding for GPT. No before-and-after test of the check on decision quality.
agent_relevance: Gap 7 answered in part: a numeric reconciliation check is cheap and catches arithmetic contradictions, but it does not anchor severity. Authors advise prescribing the severity path and using the model only for narrative.

source: Lorenz & Fritz (2026) Scalable Delphi (arXiv 2602.08889), re-read for round data
finding: No round-by-round results, no no-feedback arm, no single-pass baseline. Only final estimates after the last round are shown.
numbers: Five-expert panels; two rounds in the expert-alignment test. GPT-5.1 vs human panel A MAD 5.0 pp; Opus-4.1 12.8 pp; two human panels differ by 16.6 pp. Persona ablation MAD 3.0 pp (GPT-5.1) and 1.9 pp (Opus).
limits: Cost claim of three orders of magnitude has no figures. Confirms the critique: no ablation of rounds in this paper.
agent_relevance: Gap 1: this key paper cannot support a claim that feedback rounds matter.

source: Sela (2026) deliberation with 7-9B models (arXiv 2604.26561), re-read for rounds
finding: Feedback designs failed on small models. No one-shot majority baseline and no counts of flips.
numbers: Three debate rounds then single ranking. Exposure to peers amplified artificial consensus; two rounds of exposure compounded sycophantic flips; self-confrontation changed 0 votes in 10 runs.
limits: No token cost. No larger-model comparison.
agent_relevance: Against adding more feedback rounds for small models. Consistent with d04 where Llama-4-Scout gained only 0.005.

source: Csaszar et al. (2026) LLMs vs managers on Kickstarter (arXiv 2602.01684), re-read for scope
finding: Study is one domain and single calls. No agent scaffolds, tools or token matching.
numbers: 870 pairwise comparisons over 30 Kickstarter technology projects; temperature 0.5 where allowed; authors say they do not claim the chess moment for strategy has arrived.
limits: Appendices not read (text truncated). Preprocessing used OCR and GPT-5-High summaries.
agent_relevance: Gap 6 stays open on both counts: no other domain, no scaffold-vs-best-model at equal tokens.

finding: Adverse scenarios were set too mild before the 2011 euro crisis.
numbers: EBA 2009 and 2010 adverse euro-area growth -0.6%; revised to -4.0% for 2011. 25 banks failed the 2014 EBA test. Post-stress capital at large US banks generally rose after Dodd-Frank tests.
agent_relevance: Gap 8: no study of LLM agents using probability-anchored adverse scenarios found. Human tests show severity is hard to calibrate, same as d12.
